items.prompt: Explain which fictional health programme better fits remote communities. A funds outreach for routine care and referrals for 80% of residents. B funds a reachable district hospital and transport serving 55%, with stronger specialist capacity. Both have staff and supplies; only one can be expanded first.
items.canonical_answer: Outreach reaches more residents and can support early and preventive care, but relies on referral for specialist needs. The hospital offers more complex care and transport, but covers fewer people in the current plan. Prefer outreach where unmet routine needs dominate; prioritise hospital capacity where the evidence shows serious referral bottlenecks. The strongest long-term arrangement connects the two. A building count or one coverage figure cannot establish overall quality and need.
marking_guidance: Judgement: compare genuine benefits and costs against the stated aim.
Reason: develop each option using supplied evidence, weigh the trade-off, and give a conditional conclusion.
Original indicative practice guidance; not an official mark scheme.

items.prompt: Explain which fictional HIV-support programme better fits continued participation. A reaches more people with confidential care and transport. B reaches fewer people but also funds household care-time support. Both preserve employment access for people able to work, and only one fits the initial budget.
items.canonical_answer: A removes the travel barrier for a wider group and supports continuity of care. B addresses care burdens as well, potentially protecting both the person’s and another household member’s participation, but helps fewer households. Prefer B where care-time losses are the most serious unmet need, or A where transport excludes many people from effective services. Judge reach and the depth of support against actual needs rather than choosing exclusion as a false alternative.

items.prompt: State (a) two supports needed to turn a clinic building into usable care [2]. Explain (b) a fictional programme where a new clinic is built but no staff or medicine supply is funded and travel remains unaffordable [4].
items.canonical_answer: (a) Trained staff and dependable supplies. (b) The new building supplies space but cannot examine or treat patients without trained staff. Without a funded medicine supply, it also cannot provide treatments that depend on those medicines. Unaffordable travel can prevent residents reaching the clinic even after staffing and supplies improve. The programme therefore needs an operating budget and practical access arrangements alongside construction; assess care actually delivered and who can use it rather than counting buildings alone.
marking_guidance: Point: two valid operating supports [2].
Development: connect both missing capacity and access to the bounded programme result [4].
Original indicative practice guidance; not an official mark scheme.

items.prompt: Calculate (a) usable service coverage if 180 of 300 eligible residents can reach staffed care in a fictional district [2]. Explain (b) whether a second unstaffed building alone solves the gap when the unserved residents also lack transport [4].
items.canonical_answer: (a) 180 ÷ 300 = 0.6; multiplying by 100 gives 60%. (b) Forty percent remain uncovered, but an unstaffed building adds no operating care and does not remove transport barriers. Prioritise feasible staffing and access arrangements rather than building counts alone.
marking_guidance: Evidence: correct denominator and 60% [2].
Meaning: combine uncovered share, absent staff and transport to justify the practical priority [4].
Original indicative practice guidance; not an official mark scheme.
